name: Bouncing ball
description:
A ball thrown straight up from the floor at 20 m/s, falling back under gravity and bouncing with 0.9 of the speed it landed with: the classic test of how a solver handles events. Height is the one compartment. Bounce is a trigger that fires when Height falls through zero, so the solver stops exactly there and starts again. Each bounce takes two snapshots, its time (T_bounce) and the speed the ball leaves the floor with (V_up), and between bounces the ball's Velocity is V_up − g·(t − T_bounce).

The landing speed is read off the flight time: a flight from the floor and back takes 2V/g, so the ball lands at g times half its time in the air. That keeps V_up from reading its own value, which a snapshot may not do. The bounces come where the closed form (2·v0/g)·(1 − eⁿ)/(1 − e) puts them: 4.08, 7.75 and 11.05 s, and so on, twelve in the thirty seconds, with the energy falling to e² = 0.81 of itself at each.

Try: run it to 45 s. The bounces pile up towards (2·v0/g)/(1 − e) = 40.8 s, where infinitely many of them would happen in a finite time (Zeno behaviour). After about a hundred, the flights are too short to resolve and the ball falls through the floor. That is a property of the model, which needs a rule for coming to rest, not a fault in the solver.
